Listen to this article Now playing · 8 min For nearly two decades, the headquarters responsible for American military operations across Africa has sat not on the African continent itself but in Germany.
US Africa Command began operations in 2007 and became fully operational the following year. Stuttgart was initially only an interim solution while the Pentagon considered where to more permanently establish its newest combatant command. In 2013, the Department of Defense chose to keep it there to take advantage of established American infrastructure, proximity to US European Command, and access to AFRICOM’s component commands in Germany and Italy.
Since then, the strategic environment that made Stuttgart sensible has changed. The United States withdrew from Niger in 2024, losing an important foothold in the Sahel. Violent extremist organizations remain entrenched in the region. Russia has expanded its military involvement through its Africa Corps, while China maintains a base in Djibouti and continues to cultivate strategic relationships across the continent. Tensions surrounding critical minerals and maritime access have added further importance to Africa’s security landscape. AFRICOM’s own 2026 posture statement warns that eroding access is constraining its ability to respond to crises.
The strategic map of Africa has changed, so why hasn’t AFRICOM’s headquarters?
The United States should begin shifting AFRICOM’s center of gravity to coastal West Africa, establishing a substantial forward headquarters while retaining its assets in Stuttgart as a European support element. The objective of this move is an extension of AFRICOM’s reach onto the continent, not a severance from European resources.
Moving a headquarters to anywhere in Africa is not enough; its location on the continent needs to make sense. AFRICOM’s new home must be a workable command position, not a token change of address. North Africa is a tempting choice, but it’s too close to Europe to warrant a move across the Mediterranean. East Africa already hosts a major American presence at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, but their hands are full enough with the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Horn of Africa. The Sahel, beset by insurgency and political upheaval, is too volatile for a permanent combatant-command headquarters.
Coastal West Africa offers a more useful balance. It’s close to the problem, but not inside it.
Ghana has an established defense relationship with the United States, access to the Gulf of Guinea, and an English-speaking operating environment. Côte d’Ivoire offers substantial infrastructure around Abidjan, borders Mali and Burkina Faso, and has deepened security cooperation with Washington. Both offer proximity to the Sahel without requiring a vulnerable headquarters inside its most volatile areas. This argument is for the region, not a predetermined site. The Pentagon and State Department would need to assess feasibility and negotiate with any prospective host government.
The worst version of this proposal would be the most dramatic one where AFRICOM announces that it is leaving Stuttgart to construct another sprawling installation, transferring its entire headquarters at once. Doing so would be unnecessary, expensive, and politically reckless.
A better strategy begins with a forward command node staffed largely by rotational or unaccompanied personnel. It should be large enough to support secure communications, intelligence coordination, operational planning, logistics, and a meaningful senior leadership presence, but small enough to remain reversible. The first phase should test whether a forward staff actually improves in-theater decisions and partnerships. As that headquarters proves itself, more planning, partner engagement, and command functions could migrate from Stuttgart. Permanent support facilities should follow demonstrated need, not precede it.
Only after the African headquarters can reliably perform the mission should it become AFRICOM’s principal command node. This approach has precedent in early Defense Department planning which contemplated a forward headquarters in Africa, supported by a rear headquarters elsewhere.
Stuttgart would remain valuable even after the move to West Africa. AFRICOM’s service components are closely tied to existing European bases and support systems. A smaller rear headquarters could maintain those links, coordinate with EUCOM and NATO, while providing redundancy. If an African host government withdraws consent or security deteriorates, functions could shift back toward Stuttgart. That gives commanders freedom of maneuver rather than wagering the mission on a single location. The aim is not to transplant AFRICOM’s entire enterprise, but to move its center of gravity closer to the action.
More than merely symbolic, this move is operationally logical. A West African headquarters could give commanders more sustained contact with regional military partners, deeper familiarity with political and logistical realities, and a stronger foundation for planning near the Sahel. Uniformed and civilian specialists would gain regional knowledge through daily work rather than periodic visits from Europe. Likewise, African counterparts would have more consistent access to US decisionmakers.
An African headquarters, however, does not automatically grant access to local airfields, overflight rights, or faster responses across a vast continent. Those gains would still depend on host agreements, infrastructure, and operational decisions. The case for relocation is the cumulative value of being present, building relationships, and maintaining two command nodes rather than relying solely on Stuttgart.
Developing a serious headquarters in Africa would not be cheap. Earlier Pentagon studies identified potential costs for housing, communications, medical care, and other infrastructure. The Pentagon nevertheless kept AFRICOM in Stuttgart despite cheaper alternatives because senior leaders judged its operational advantages worth the expense. As attested by those who remember HESCOs and tents from the War on Terror, the cheapest headquarters is not necessarily the best headquarters.
That same logic deserves consideration today, but spending must be incremental. Congress should weigh each phase against measurable gains in access, coordination, and resilience, not merely the visibility of an American flag on African soil. A larger military footprint cannot substitute for diplomacy, development, or trade; it must serve a broader American Africa policy with transparent host-nation consent.
Moving can be a pain, but it’s often a necessary one. Delaying the inevitable inconvenience isn’t the answer. Stuttgart was a reasonable answer to past circumstances, but it’s time now to put AFRICOM in Africa. America needs to build forward, preserve its European backbone, and shift responsibilities only when the African headquarters proves it can carry them.
The strategic map has changed. AFRICOM’s posture should change with it.
